title: M-DESIGN: Evidence-Guided Neural Network Refinement
one_liner: Search for better neural networks by reusing evidence of what architecture changes worked on similar past tasks.
lead: Building a good neural network for a new task usually means either running an expensive search (trying many variants and picking the best) or grabbing a pre-trained model that may not fit. M-DESIGN solves this by storing what architectural changes (like adding layers, changing connection patterns, or adjusting weights and numbers in the network) improved performance on past tasks, then using that historical evidence to guide a quick search on the new task.

problem.h2: The old way is slow or stuck
paras: To build a neural network, you set up the architecture (how many layers, what types of operations), train it on data, and measure how well it works. If performance is bad, most people either throw it out and try a totally different architecture from scratch (neural architecture search, which tries thousands of variants and takes hours), or they grab a pre-trained network someone published that worked well on a similar task (model retrieval, which is fast but often does not fit your data).

The trap is this: once you find a pre-trained network that works okay for your task, you face a problem. Without a record of which small changes helped on similar tasks in the past, you cannot learn from history. Your only options are to guess (making random changes and hoping), or run a fresh expensive search over thousands of variants.

callout.html: M-DESIGN records which small architectural changes (adding or removing components, changing how pieces connect) improved the network on past similar tasks, then uses that record to guide a fast search for the best changes on a new task.

steps.text: For each past task, record which small architectural changes improved performance and by how much.
Test a few past edits on the new task to see which still work. Some edits that boosted old tasks may fail on the new one because the task structure is different, so test first.
Rank edits by how often they improved past tasks similar to this one, adjusted down for edits that are failing on this new task. Higher-ranked edits get tried first.
Layer on the top-ranked changes and retrain the network on the new task.
Because the changes come from real evidence, the search stops much sooner than blind architecture search.

paras: M-DESIGN changes the path of architectural modifications (which edits to try and in what order) by pulling information from past successful edits rather than guessing.

hidden.name: edit-effect evidence score
paras: When you modify a neural network for a graph task (say, adding a new kind of layer or changing how neurons connect), the performance either jumps up, stays flat, or drops. M-DESIGN measures this effect for each small change on each past task and stores it: a table of 'edit X on task A gained 4%, edit Y on task A lost 1%, edit X on task B gained 2%.' This is the evidence.

On a new task, M-DESIGN estimates transferability (will an edit that helped before still help now?) by checking how similar the new task is to the old ones. If the new task has the same types of nodes and connections as the past tasks, then edits that boosted the old networks are likely to boost this one too, because the networks face the same challenge. If the new task looks very different, the paper lowers its confidence in the historical edits.

heat.caption: Darker: edit gave bigger performance gain on that task. Boxes: edits that transferred to other tasks.

reads.html: Past architectural edits are scored by how much they improved the network. You pick edits that scored well on similar old tasks to test first on your new task.

M-DESIGN stores performance gains from 67,760 graph neural networks and retrieves the top-scoring evidence from tasks similar to the new one, then weights each historical edit by a learned transferability score that decreases if the new task becomes too different from the average.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: Architectural search usually fails because there are too many possible edits to try in a reasonable time. M-DESIGN shrinks the search space by filtering edits through historical evidence: it only tests edits that have a track record of working, in an order ranked by past success. This cuts the search space from millions of variants down to dozens of promising ones.

Second, the paper handles the problem that 'helpful on the old task' does not always mean 'helpful on the new one' by measuring transferability on the fly. As the new task gets clearer (after a few experiments), M-DESIGN adjusts its confidence in each piece of historical evidence. Edits that seemed promising but are failing get downweighted; edits that keep working get trusted more. This adaptive update keeps the search focused on what actually works for this task, not just a generic neighbor.

Third, the paper uses a predictive step to handle uncertainty. Rather than require a massive repository of every possible edit on every past task (impossible), it trains a small model that can look at a sequence of edits and guess the total performance gain if all are applied together. This 'multi-hop' prediction lets it extrapolate beyond the stored evidence, reducing pressure to have seen every case before.

stages.s: New graph task + pre-trained base model
Find similar past tasks in the evidence store
Rank edits by historical success on those neighbors
Test top-ranked edits on the new task
Update transferability scores as real results come in
Best model found within the budget

math.words: The adjusted score for edit E on the new task is the historical gain from E multiplied by a weight that reflects how much the new task resembles the past tasks where E was tested, scaled down if the new task drifts too far from the average.
symbols: average performance gain from edit E across past tasks where it was tried
fraction from 0 to 1; how much the new task looks like the past ones
how different the new task is from the center of past tasks (in feature space)
how far the new task can drift before edits stop being trusted (a tuning constant)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Edit A (add a new connection type) gave average gain of 3% on past graph tasks.
The new task is 30% similar to past ones (transferability weight = 0.30).
The new task drifts 0.5 units away, scale = 1.0, so exp(-0.5/1.0) = 0.61.
Compare to Edit B which gained only 1% before: 1% * 0.30 * 0.61 = 0.18%.
Edit A is ranked first; the search tries it first.

math.note: When an edit worked well in the past and the new task resembles those past tasks closely, the score stays high and the search tries that edit immediately. As the new task becomes different or an edit fails on it, scores drop and the search tries other edits instead.

items.b: Task too different from the past.
items.html: If the new graph task is unlike anything in the history (different size, different types of nodes, a problem the store has never seen), the past edits may not transfer. M-DESIGN will try them anyway and waste budget. The paper handles this by measuring how far the new task sits from the store's average, then downweighting old evidence when the distance grows, but if the task is far enough, the method behaves like blind search.

M-DESIGN relies on past data. Starting on a new domain (say, protein graphs when the store has only citation graphs), the method has little evidence to draw from and starts weak, because there are few historical edits to measure. Each new task added to the store makes future searches faster, because there is more history to learn from.

If the predictive model that guesses multi-hop gains is trained on the same store it reads from, it may memorize past quirks and overestimate gains on the new task. The paper guards this with a held-out validation set, but mistakes are possible.

M-DESIGN works best when the new task stays within the domain of past tasks (e.g., adding a new graph neural network problem to a library of graph problems), the evidence store has many examples with clear records of which edits helped, and the search budget is moderate (not forced to decide in 2 trials, not planning to try 10,000 variants).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should build a small evidence store from 3-5 graph tasks (like citation networks, social graphs, or protein interactions), record which small edits (adding layers, changing a connection pattern, dropping a component) improved each one. Then, given a new graph task not in the store, run M-DESIGN to search for the best model, and compare it to two baselines: (1) a blind search that tries random edits, (2) just using the best pre-trained model from the store without refinement. The demo should show M-DESIGN finding a good model in far fewer trials than blind search.
demo.closing: The payoff is clear when M-DESIGN reaches 85% accuracy in 50 trials, blind search needs 400 trials, and the pre-trained baseline caps out at 78%.
